en: Llama, Mistral and OLMo all run the same three-matrix trick.
And Llama and OLMo pay for it by shrinking that layer to about two-thirds. Why would anyone do that?
From Professor Yufei Ding's CSE 291P at UC San Diego: the gate.
A matrix multiply turns a list of numbers into a new list of weighted sums.
Layers like that are linear. Stack as many as you like: together they are still one matrix multiply.
One straight-line map, like straight rulers on a wavy curve. Her class demo:
So between them goes a bend: a non-linearity, also called an activation function.
In 1991, Kurt Hornik proved that one hidden layer, with a bounded non-linear activation and enough units,
can get as close as you like to any continuous function on a bounded region. A 1993 follow-up covered ReLU too.
It promises that such a network exists, not that training will find it.
Inside a transformer, the design behind these models, the activation sits in one place: the feed-forward layer. In her words:
In letters: FFN of x equals act of x W1, times W2.
Each token, a word or a piece of one, arrives as h numbers, the model width. The first matrix widens it to 4h, the hidden width.
Picture the activation as a kitchen tap. The water is the content. The hand on the tap is the gate.
The 2017 Transformer used ReLU: positive numbers pass as they are, negative numbers become zero.
Shut or fully open: a switch. Minus one goes in, zero comes out.
Training nudges each weight using slopes, called gradients. ReLU's slope is one for positives, zero for negatives.
But if a unit outputs zero for every input, its slope is zero everywhere.
No learning signal ever reaches it, so it never grows: a dead ReLU.
So, a dimmer instead of a switch. GELU multiplies x by Phi of x.
Phi of x is the chance a bell-curve sample falls below x: near one for big x, near zero for very negative x.
The water sets the tap by itself: a strong flow opens it, a negative trickle mostly shuts it.
Her slide 17, with our own curves. Minus one now comes out as minus 0.16: a trickle, so it still gets a gradient.
BERT and the first GPT used GELU. It costs more than ReLU, but beside the matrix multiplies it is small change.
A sigmoid squeezes any number into an S-curve between zero and one. Its slope never tops one quarter.
But as a hand on the tap, it works. x times sigmoid of x: SiLU, the Sigmoid Linear Unit.
Cheaper than GELU: minus one comes out as minus 0.27. And it was already in the 2016 GELU paper.
In 2017, a Google Brain team let a computer search through combinations of simple functions.
Swish came out on top: x times sigmoid of beta x. With beta at one, it is exactly SiLU.
So far, the water turns its own tap: the same x is both the water and the hand.
A gated linear unit gives the tap to a second person: two separate matrix multiplies of the same input.
One makes the water. A sigmoid of the other decides, number by number, how much of that water gets through.
SwiGLU, Swish plus GLU, gives that hand a SiLU: SiLU of x W, times x V, then W2.
Three matrices: one makes the gate, one makes the content, one brings the result back down.
On her slide 20, the pen fixes one word: SwiGLU's gate is SiLU, as the figure on her own slide says.
Llama, Mistral and OLMo all use SwiGLU. Gemma uses a GELU-gated cousin, GeGLU.
Her slide 21 keeps score. Cheap forward? Cheap gradient? ReLU: yes, yes. GELU: no, no. SiLU: so-so.
Healthy gradients? Not ReLU. And her last row: today's winners run SiLU, mostly as SwiGLU, like Llama, Mistral and OLMo.
Better, but only a little: about 1.68 against 1.64 on the paper's score, lower is better.
And why does it work? The paper ends:
“We offer no explanation as to why these architectures seem to work; we attribute their success, as all else, to divine benevolence.”
Now the bill. Each matrix entry is a weight the model learns, a parameter.
A plain layer: two matrices of h by 4h, 8 h-squared weights. A third one at the same width makes 12 h-squared.
Each weight costs about two operations per token, a multiply and an add. More weights, more compute.
Three matrices of h by the new width hold 3 times h times that width. Set that equal to 8 h-squared.
The new width comes out at 8 thirds of h: two-thirds of 4h, about 2.67 h. Same weights, same compute.
In Llama's 7B model, 4h would be 16,384. Two-thirds is about 10,923; the code rounds up to 11,008. OLMo's 7B lands on the same 11,008.
Back to the puzzle: one matrix for the water, one for the hand, one for the way back.
A switch, then a dimmer, then a second pair of hands.
